subject: Climate & Environment
title: Rare Earth Minerals and Conflict
description: A quick win: understand Rare Earth Minerals and Conflict.

hook.text: Your smartphone contains about 30 different elements — many mined under brutal conditions.

buildup.text: Cobalt for batteries comes largely from the Congo, where child labor is widespread in mines.

discovery.text: Rare earth elements are essential for electronics, wind turbines, and electric car motors.

twist.text: China controls about 60% of rare earth mining and 90% of processing — a geopolitical risk.

climax.text: Recycling e-waste could supply many of these minerals — reducing both mining and waste.

punchline.text: Our clean future depends on some of the dirtiest supply chains on Earth.

quiz.question: Which country dominates rare earth mineral processing?

details.summary: Rare earth minerals essential for electronics, batteries, and renewable energy are mined under conditions that often involve environmental destruction, child labor, and conflict.
details.whyItMatters: The green energy transition depends on these minerals. Ensuring ethical sourcing and recycling is critical to prevent clean technology from perpetuating exploitation and environmental harm.
takeaways: Rare earth mining often involves environmental devastation
Child labor and conflict fund some mineral supply chains
Recycling e-waste can reduce demand for new mining

faq.question: Why is cobalt mining controversial?
faq.answer: Over 70 percent of global cobalt comes from the DRC, where artisanal mines often use child labor in dangerous conditions. Workers dig by hand in unregulated tunnels with no safety equipment. Investigations have linked major electronics brands to these supply chains.

faq.question: Can recycling reduce the need for new mining?
faq.answer: Yes. Urban mining, which recovers metals from discarded electronics, can supply a growing share of demand. A smartphone contains over 30 elements. If global e-waste recycling rates doubled, it could significantly reduce pressure on primary extraction and associated harms.
